On $\Omega_R=\Omega\cap\{r<R\}$ the unknowns are $f,Z$. Define $t$ implicitly and the remaining variables explicitly by <a id="four:maximal:def:axial-variables"></a><a id="four:maximal:def:weights"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \sigma&=|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f|,& D&=1+l(t)^2\sigma^2,&d&=D^{-1},
 & Z&=t+\tfrac16\log D,\label{four:maximal:def:implicit}\\
 w&=\frac{l\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f}{\sqrt D},&a&=|w|,&v&=a^2=1-d,
 &\chi&=\frac{3d}{3+pv},\label{four:maximal:def:axial-variables}\\
 h&=\eta_N f,&U&=l\sqrt D,&u&=L_0\sqrt D.
 \label{four:maximal:def:weights}
\end{aligned}$$ At fixed $\sigma$, the derivative of the right side of <a href="#four:maximal:def:implicit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:implicit">[four:maximal:def:implicit]</a> with respect to $t$ is $1+pv/3>0$. As $t\to-\infty$ it tends to $-\infty$, and as $t\to\infty$ it tends to $\infty$. Consequently $t=t(Z,df)$ exists uniquely and smoothly for all finite arguments. Notice that $t\ge-\epsilon$ implies $\ell\le l\le e$.

<a id="four:maximal:def:trace"></a>
For $\sigma>0$ put $e_f=\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f/\sigma$ and $A_j=\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}+(j-1)e_f\otimes e_f$. The two matrices used below have the globally smooth formulas <a id="four:maximal:def:matrices"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:matrices}
 A_d=\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}-w\otimes w,\qquad
 A_\chi=\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}-\frac{3+p}{3+pv}w\otimes w,
 \qquad \frac{3d}{3+N}\le\chi\le d\le1.$$ They are positive definite; the displayed formulas remove the apparent ambiguity of the axis when $df=0$. We identify vectors and covectors using $g$, write $|\xi|_A^2=A(\xi,\xi)$, and put <a id="four:maximal:def:graph-fields"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:graph-fields}
 \begin{gathered}
 \bar g=g+l^2df\otimes df,\quad
 \widehat g=e^{2t}\bar g,\quad
 H^f=\frac{l}{\sqrt D}\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f,\quad S_f=K+H^f,\\
 V=uA_\chi\bigl(3\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Z+K(w,\cdot)\bigr).
 \end{gathered}$$ The trace equation will always be $$\label{four:maximal:def:trace}
 \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}S_f=F.$$ Here $F$ is the prescribed right side, including its dependence on $f$, $Z$, and $df$ when a system is specified.

For symmetric tensors recall $P_A=A-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}A)g$ and $\mathsf{B}(A_1,A_2)=A_1:A_2-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}A_1)(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}A_2)$. The constraint quantities are $\mu=(R_g-\mathsf{B}(K,K))/2$ and $J=\mathop{\mathrm{div}}P_K$. At a point with $\sigma>0$, decompose $S_f$ relative to $e_f^\perp\oplus\mathbb Re_f$ into its transverse symmetric block $T$, mixed covector $M$, and axial entry $j$. The letter $M$ in the formulas below denotes only this block. Put <a id="four:maximal:def:blocks"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:blocks}
 x=\partial_{e_f}t,\qquad y=(\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}t)_\perp,
 \qquad T^0=T-\tfrac13(F-\chi j)\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}_\perp.$$ The trace equation gives $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}T=F-\chi j$.

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-prop-scalar-identity"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:prop:scalar-identity" class="proposition">

<a id="four:maximal:def:quadratic-form"></a>
**Proposition 44** (Scalar identity). *For smooth $f,t$ satisfying <a href="#four:maximal:def:trace" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:trace">[four:maximal:def:trace]</a>, <a id="four:maximal:def:scalar-identity"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:scalar-identity}
 \frac12 e^{2t}R_{\widehat g}
 =\mu+J(w)+\mathcal T+w(F)-F\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}K-u^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}V,$$ where $$\begin{aligned}
\label{four:maximal:def:quadratic-form}
 \mathcal T={}&\tfrac12|T^0|^2+|M+(p+1)ay|^2-v|y|^2
       +3(p+1)(|y|^2+dx^2)\notag\\
 &-\tfrac13(F-\chi j)^2+\chi j^2-\chi Fj+F^2
       +2(p+1)\chi jax.
\end{aligned}$$ This expression extends smoothly across $df=0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-prop-scalar-identity"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-prop-scalar-identity</summary>

*Proof.* This is Proposition [four:sys:scalar-proposition], with its axis $e=e_f$ and the same graph variables and density normalization. Its arbitrary trace $\tau$ is zero here.

We record the differential relations needed in the boundary and drift calculations. Differentiating the implicit definition of $Z$ gives <a id="four:maximal:def:Z-differential"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:Z-differential}
 3\,dZ=(3+pv)dt+H^f(w,\cdot).$$ If $k=-H^f-p(dt\otimes w^\flat+w^\flat\otimes dt)$ and $Q=K-k$, then <a id="four:maximal:def:flux-rewrite"></a><a id="four:maximal:def:w-divergence"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 V/u&=P_Qw+3A_d\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}t+Fw,
                    \label{four:maximal:def:flux-rewrite}\\
 u^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(uw)
 &=F+(1-\chi)j-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_gK+2(p+1)w(t).
                    \label{four:maximal:def:w-divergence}
\end{aligned}$$ These are the identities in the proof of the cited proposition. They follow by inserting $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}T=F-\chi j$ and $H^f(w,\cdot)=v\,d\log\sigma$ into its invariant formula; their smooth tensor expressions also hold at $df=0$. The quadratic expression there is precisely the displayed $\mathcal T$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-lem-coercivity"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:lem:coercivity" class="lemma">

<a id="four:maximal:def:coercivity"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:def:coercivity-stationary"></a>
**Lemma 45** (Polynomial coercivity). *The quadratic form in <a href="#four:maximal:def:quadratic-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:quadratic-form">[four:maximal:def:quadratic-form]</a> is nonnegative, and $$\label{four:maximal:def:coercivity}
 |T|^2+|M|^2+dj^2+F^2+|dt|_{A_d}^2\le\Pi_N\mathcal T.$$ At $dt=0$ it has the stronger equivalence $$\label{four:maximal:def:coercivity-stationary}
 \mathcal T\asymp |T^0|^2+|M|^2+\chi j^2+F^2,$$ with both constants absolute, independent of $N,d,\chi$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-lem-coercivity"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-lem-coercivity</summary>

*Proof.* Lemma [four:sys:coercivity-lemma] applies with the same dictionary. For clarity, its exact square completion is <a id="four:maximal:def:square-completion"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
\label{four:maximal:def:square-completion}
 \mathcal T={}&\tfrac12|T^0|^2+|M+(p+1)ay|^2
       +\bigl(3(p+1)-v\bigr)|y|^2\notag\\
 &+3(p+1)d\left(x+\frac{\chi aj}{3d}\right)^2
       +\tfrac23\left(F-\frac{\chi j}{4}\right)^2
       +\frac{d(48-3d)}{8(3+pv)^2}j^2.
\end{aligned}$$ The last coefficient is at least $45d/[8(3+N)^2]$ and the coefficient of $|y|^2$ is at least two. Undoing the shifted squares therefore costs only a polynomial in $N$. When $dt=0$, the normal terms instead reduce to $$\tfrac23(F-\chi j/4)^2+\chi(1-3\chi/8)j^2.$$ The bounds $5/8\le1-3\chi/8\le1$ and $\chi^2\le\chi$ give the absolute equivalence claimed in <a href="#four:maximal:def:coercivity-stationary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:coercivity-stationary">[four:maximal:def:coercivity-stationary]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-lem-boundary-identity"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:lem:boundary-identity" class="lemma">

<a id="four:maximal:def:boundary-flux"></a>
**Lemma 46** (Boundary identity). *On a hypersurface where $f$ is constant, let $H$ denote its $g$-mean curvature for a chosen normal $\nu$, and put $P_B=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_BK$. Then <a id="four:maximal:def:boundary-curvature"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 V_\nu/u&=d(H+3\partial_\nu t)-H+w_\nu(F-P_B),
 \label{four:maximal:def:boundary-flux}\\
 \widehat H&=e^{-t}\sqrt d\,(H+3\partial_\nu t).
 \label{four:maximal:def:boundary-curvature}
\end{aligned}$$ The identities allow either sign of $\partial_\nu f$, including zero.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-lem-boundary-identity"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-lem-boundary-identity</summary>

*Proof.* Apply Lemma [four:sys:boundary-lemma] with the chosen normal $\nu$ and trace relation <a href="#four:maximal:def:trace" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:trace">[four:maximal:def:trace]</a>. Its formulas use the signed component $w_\nu$ and extend smoothly to $df=0$, so they also apply when the normal graph slope changes sign. ◻

</details>

<a id="four:maximal:def:homotopy"></a>
#### The equations and their homotopy

<a id="four:maximal:def:penalty"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:def:boundary-datum"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:def:system"></a>
Choose <a id="four:maximal:def:end-weights"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:end-weights}
 1<\gamma<\min(2,q-\delta/2),\qquad
 \rho_0=r^{-4-\delta},\qquad \rho_1=r^{-2\gamma}.$$ Here $r$ is the fixed positive smooth extension of the end radius. Fix smooth cutoffs $m_0^*,j_0:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ with $m_0^*=1$ on $(-\infty,0]$, $m_0^*=0$ on $[1,\infty)$, $j_0=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$, and $j_0=1$ on $[1,\infty)$. Define $$\label{four:maximal:def:penalty}
 \mathcal P=C_N(\rho_0+v\rho_1),\qquad
 m_0(t)=m_0^*(N(t+\epsilon)),\qquad
 \Xi=\delta_0\mathcal T+\rho+\delta_0\eta_N a\sigma-m_0(t)\mathcal P.$$ Proposition <a href="#four:maximal:prop:floor" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:prop:floor">50</a> below fixes a single $\delta_0>0$ independent of $N$ and then a sufficiently large polynomial $C_N$. Choose a smooth $N_B>1+\sup_B|H|$ on $B$ and write $$\label{four:maximal:def:boundary-datum}
 \mathcal B=-H+w_\nu(F-P_B)-N_Bd,\qquad P_B=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_BK.$$ The system whose solution we seek is $$\label{four:maximal:def:system}
 \begin{cases}
  \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}(K+H^f)=F=h+C,&\text{in }\Omega_R,\\
  \mathop{\mathrm{div}}V=u\Xi,&\text{in }\Omega_R,\\
  h=b_*,\quad V_\nu/u=\mathcal B,&\text{on }B,\\
  f=Z=0,&\text{on }S_R.
 \end{cases}$$ In the boundary datum, $F$ always means the prescribed trace right side, so the datum contains no unprescribed second derivatives.

The two geometric signs follow directly for any smooth solution of <a href="#four:maximal:def:system" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:system">[four:maximal:def:system]</a>. Maximality and Proposition <a href="#four:maximal:prop:scalar-identity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:prop:scalar-identity">44</a> give the exact decomposition <a id="four:maximal:def:scalar-sign"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:scalar-sign}
 \frac12e^{2t}R_{\widehat g}
 =\bigl(\mu+J(w)+w(C)-\rho\bigr)
  +(1-\delta_0)\mathcal T+(1-\delta_0)\eta_N a\sigma+m_0\mathcal P.$$ The bracket is nonnegative by <a href="#four:maximal:def:slack" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:slack">[four:maximal:def:slack]</a> and $|w|\le1$, and all other terms are nonnegative when $\delta_0<1$. On $B$, subtracting <a href="#four:maximal:def:boundary-datum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:boundary-datum">[four:maximal:def:boundary-datum]</a> from <a href="#four:maximal:def:boundary-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:boundary-flux">[four:maximal:def:boundary-flux]</a> gives $H+3\partial_\nu t=-N_B$, and therefore <a id="four:maximal:def:geometric-signs"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:geometric-signs}
 R_{\widehat g}\ge0,\qquad \widehat H=-e^{-t}\sqrt d\,N_B<0.$$ These conclusions use the actual boundary expansion $H+P_B=b_*$. They require no assumption that $H$ vanishes.

<a id="four:maximal:def:homotopy-boundary"></a>
Here is a homotopy to a scalar system with a trivial endpoint. Let $$V_\lambda=uA_\chi\bigl(3\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Z+\lambda K(w,\cdot)\bigr),
 \qquad 0\le\lambda\le1.$$ In the first three stages impose $\mathop{\mathrm{div}}V_\lambda=u\Xi$ and $$\label{four:maximal:def:homotopy-boundary}
 \frac{(V_\lambda)_\nu}{u}
 =\bigl[1-(1-\lambda)j_0(t)\bigr]
   \bigl[\mathcal B-(1-\lambda)
                (A_\chi K(w,\cdot))_\nu\bigr].$$ All outer values remain $f=Z=0$. Let $\nu_s=\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}s/|ds|$ in the fixed collars. Choose smooth bounded functions $D_0(x,w)$ and $D_1(x,w)$, supported in those collars and with uniformly bounded derivatives for $|w|\le1$, as follows:

- $D_0\le0$, $D_0=0$ when $w\cdot \nu_s\ge0$, and $D_0(x,-\nu)<-2\sup_B|H|$ on $B$;

- $D_1=A_1\zeta_B(x)w\cdot \nu_s$, where $\zeta_B=1$ near $B$ is a fixed collar cutoff and $A_1>1+\sup_B|H|$.

Such $D_0$ is obtained by a fixed smooth function of $w\cdot \nu_s$, zero on the nonnegative half-line and sufficiently negative at $-1$, times a collar cutoff. In particular $D_0(x,0)=D_1(x,0)=0$. The stages, with their endpoints included, are:

1.  Decrease $\lambda$ from one to zero, keeping $F=h+C$ and $h|_B=b_*$.

2.  Keep $\lambda=0$ and increase $\alpha$ from zero to one, with $F=h+C+\alpha D_0$ and $h|_B=b_*$.

3.  Keep $\lambda=0$ and increase $\zeta$ from zero to one, with <a id="four:maximal:def:stage-three"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:stage-three}
      F=h+(1-\zeta)(C+D_0)
           +\zeta\bigl(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}K+D_1\bigr),
      \qquad h|_B=(1-\zeta)b_*.$$

4.  Keep the terminal trace problem <a id="four:maximal:def:terminal-trace"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:terminal-trace}
      \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}H^f=h+D_1,\qquad f|_{B\cup S_R}=0,$$ and multiply both $\Xi$ and the right side of <a href="#four:maximal:def:homotopy-boundary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:homotopy-boundary">[four:maximal:def:homotopy-boundary]</a> by a common factor $\eta$, decreasing from one to zero.

The prescriptions agree at every junction. In every stage the derivative of $F$ with respect to $h$ is one. The form $\mathcal T$ is always computed from the actual trace equation and the actual tensor $K+H^f$, including when $\lambda=0$.

<a id="four:maximal:def:face-direction-signs"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:def:terminal-reduction"></a>
Two features of this choice will be used in the estimates. First, in stage three the limiting values at $w=\nu,-\nu$, with $\chi=0$ and the assigned face height, obey $$\label{four:maximal:def:face-direction-signs}
 F(x,\nu)\ge P_B+H,\qquad F(x,-\nu)\le P_B-H.$$ At $\zeta=0$ the first equality follows from $b_*=P_B+H$ and $D_0(x,\nu)=C|_B=0$; the second follows from the choice of $D_0$. At $\zeta=1$ the two values are $P_B\pm A_1$. Convex combination proves <a href="#four:maximal:def:face-direction-signs" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:face-direction-signs">[four:maximal:def:face-direction-signs]</a> for intermediate $\zeta$. Second, the terminal trace equation forces $f=0$ for every $C^{1,\alpha}$ trial $Z$ and its classical trace solution: at a positive interior maximum the left side is nonpositive and the right side is $\eta_N f>0$, while at a negative interior minimum the signs reverse. Boundary values are zero. Thus in stage four $$\label{four:maximal:def:terminal-reduction}
 f=0,\quad t=Z,\quad d=\chi=1,\quad u=L_0(t),\quad
 \mathcal T=\tfrac12|K|^2+3(p+1)|dt|^2.$$

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-lem-height-end"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:lem:height-end" class="lemma">

<a id="four:maximal:def:height-end"></a>
**Lemma 47** (Height and initial end bounds). *Every smooth homotopy solution satisfies $|h|+|F|\le C_0$ for a fixed constant independent of $N,R$ and the homotopy parameter. There are fixed $r_0,C_2$ such that, for all sufficiently large $R$ depending on $N,\epsilon$, the first three stages satisfy $$\label{four:maximal:def:height-end}
 |h|\le C_2(r^{-\gamma}-R^{-\gamma})\quad(r_0\le r\le R),
 \qquad |\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f|\big|_{S_R}\le C_3\eta_N^{-1}R^{-1-\gamma}.$$ Moreover $t>-\epsilon$ on $S_R$. None of these assertions assumes an interior lower bound for $t$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-lem-height-end"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-lem-height-end</summary>

*Proof.* At an interior extremum of $h$, we have $w=0$, $A_\chi=\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}$, $D_0=D_1=0$, and $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}K=0$. The trace equation and its positive Hessian coefficient show that a minimum has $h\ge0$ and that a maximum has $h\le\|C\|_\infty$. The boundary heights lie in $[b_*,0]$. Consequently <a id="four:maximal:def:height-range"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:height-range}
 b_*\le h\le\|C\|_\infty$$ in stages one through three; stage four has $f=0$. All remaining terms in the trace prescriptions are uniformly bounded for $|w|\le1$, $0\le\chi\le1$, so $F$ has a fixed bound as well.

<a id="four:maximal:def:K-trace-estimate"></a>
Outside the compact supports the trace equation takes the form $$\beta\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}h+s_K\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}K=h,
 \qquad \beta=\frac{l}{\eta_N\sqrt D},\qquad 0\le s_K\le1.$$ Here $s_K=1$ in the first two stages and $s_K=1-\zeta$ in the third. At a nonzero test gradient $\beta=a/|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}h|$. Test with $\psi=C_2(r^{-\gamma}-R^{-\gamma})$. Since the test axis is radial, the end metric estimates give, uniformly for $0<\chi\le1$, $$\frac{\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}\psi}{|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}\psi|}
 =\frac{-3+(\gamma+1)\chi}{r}+O(r^{-1-q})
 \le-\frac{c_1}{r},\qquad c_1=(2-\gamma)/2>0,$$ after fixing $r_0$ sufficiently large. In addition, maximality gives $$\label{four:maximal:def:K-trace-estimate}
 |\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}K|
 \le K_0r^{-1-q}\min(1,(1+N/3)a^2).$$ Indeed $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}K=(\chi-1)K(e_f,e_f)$ and $1-\chi=(3+p)v/(3+pv)\le\min(1,(1+N/3)v)$. These estimates hold for every value of <a id="pm-cite-59"></a>[[GilbargTrudinger2001](#ref-GilbargTrudinger2001), Chs. 6–9]$t$.

Put $c_\gamma=1-2^{-\gamma}$ and $H_0=\max(|b_*|,\|C\|_\infty)$. Choose the fixed coefficient $C_2$ so that $$C_2\ge\max\left\{1,
 \frac{2H_0r_0^\gamma}{c_\gamma},
 \frac{2K_0r_0^{\gamma-1-q}}{c_\gamma}\right\}.$$ For $R\ge2r_0$, this dominates the heights at $r=r_0$. On $r\le R/2$, the tensor term in <a href="#four:maximal:def:K-trace-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:K-trace-estimate">[four:maximal:def:K-trace-estimate]</a> is at most $\psi/2$, since $\gamma<1+q$. On $r\ge R/2$, use $\min(1,(1+N/3)a^2)\le\sqrt{1+N/3}\,a$ and require $$R\ge2\left(\frac{2K_0\sqrt{1+N/3}}{c_1}\right)^{1/q}.$$ The tensor error is then at most $c_1a/(2r)$.

If $h-\psi$ had a positive maximum, it would occur in the interior of this annulus. The gradients there agree and the Hessian of $h$ is no larger than the Hessian of $\psi$. The coefficients use the actual $Z$ and this common gradient, so they agree at the contact regardless of the two heights. On the first half of the annulus the equation gives $h\le-c_1a/r+\psi/2<\psi$; on the second half it gives $h\le-c_1a/(2r)<0$. Both are contradictions. At a negative minimum of $h+\psi$ the Hessian inequality reverses, while its axis and $\chi$ are unchanged on reversing the gradient; the same estimates give the lower comparison. This proves the height bound in <a href="#four:maximal:def:height-end" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:height-end">[four:maximal:def:height-end]</a>.

Because $h=0$ at $S_R$, the two comparisons bound its normal derivative there by $C_3R^{-1-\gamma}$, with $C_3=2C_2\gamma$ after increasing $r_0$ so that $|dr|\le2$. Tangential derivatives vanish, giving the asserted bound for $|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f|$. Finally, at $S_R$ the strictly increasing function $G(t)=t+\frac16\log(1+l(t)^2\sigma^2)$ has $G(t)=Z=0$. Since $l(-\epsilon)=\ell$, its root exceeds $-\epsilon$ whenever $\ell^2\sigma^2<e^{6\epsilon}-1$. It suffices to require <a id="four:maximal:def:outer-radius-floor"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:outer-radius-floor}
 R^{2\gamma+2}>
 \frac{C_3^2e^{\epsilon N}}{e^{6\epsilon}-1}.$$ In stage four the conclusion follows instead from $f=0$ and $Z=0$ on $S_R$. Every restriction on $R$ made here depends only on the fixed data, $N,\epsilon$, and is compatible with $R\to\infty$ at fixed $N$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-59"></a>
#### Exclusion of the lower boundary of the admissible range

The next argument concerns any smooth homotopy solution whose minimum value of $t$ is $-\epsilon$. It supplies the strict exclusion needed for continuation before any global gradient or Hessian estimate is available.

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-def-gauss-minimum"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:def:gauss-minimum" class="lemma">

<a id="four:maximal:def:graph-gauss"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:def:gauss-form"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:def:floor-comparison"></a>
**Lemma 48** (Gauss comparison at a minimum). *At an interior minimum of $t$, $$\label{four:maximal:def:graph-gauss}
 \tfrac12e^{2t}R_{\widehat g}
 \le\tfrac12R_g-v\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g(e_f,e_f)+\mathcal S(H^f),$$ where, for a symmetric tensor $A$, $$\label{four:maximal:def:gauss-form}
 \mathcal S(A)=\tfrac13(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\perp A)^2
 -\tfrac12|A_\perp^0|^2
 +dA_{ee}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\perp A-d|A_{e\perp}|^2.$$ At every point where $dt=0$, there is an absolute $c_2>0$ such that $$\label{four:maximal:def:floor-comparison}
 \mathcal T-\mathcal S(H^f)
 \ge c_2\mathcal T-\Pi_N\bigl(vF^2+|K|^2\bigr).$$ At $df=0$ the terms multiplied by $v$ vanish and any axis may be used.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-def-gauss-minimum"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-def-gauss-minimum</summary>

*Proof.* Lemma [four:sys:gauss-lemma], with $e=e_f$, uses exactly <a href="#four:maximal:def:gauss-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:gauss-form">[four:maximal:def:gauss-form]</a>. At a minimum $\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}t\ge0$, so its stationary Gauss identity gives <a href="#four:maximal:def:graph-gauss" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:graph-gauss">[four:maximal:def:graph-gauss]</a>.

The two algebraic identities used by its floor estimate specialize to <a id="four:maximal:def:gauss-difference"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
\label{four:maximal:def:gauss-difference}
 \mathcal T-\mathcal S(S_f)
 ={}&|T^0|^2+(1+d)|M|^2\notag\\
 &+\chi(1+d-2\chi/3)j^2+(\chi/3-d)Fj+F^2/3
\end{aligned}$$ and <a id="four:maximal:def:d-chi-ratio"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:d-chi-ratio}
 \frac{d^2}{\chi}=\frac{d(3+pv)}3\le\frac{N+3}3.$$ They are [four:sys:stationary-difference] and the first ratio in [four:sys:polynomial-ratios]. The common proof splits at $(1+p)v$ small, uses stationary coercivity, and replaces $S_f$ by $H^f=S_f-K$. It yields an absolute positive $c_2$ and a polynomial $\Pi_N$ in precisely <a href="#four:maximal:def:floor-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:floor-comparison">[four:maximal:def:floor-comparison]</a>, including the smooth extension to $df=0$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-def-coefficient-lemma"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:def:coefficient-lemma" class="lemma">

<a id="four:maximal:def:derivative-bounds"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:def:drift-divergence"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:def:F-derivative"></a>
**Lemma 49** (Coefficient derivatives). *The following estimates hold along every smooth trace solution: $$\label{four:maximal:def:derivative-bounds}
 |\nabla w|+|\nabla A_\chi|+|d\log u|_{A_\chi}
 \le\Pi_N(\sqrt{\mathcal T}+|K|).$$ Consequently, for each fixed $\eta_1>0$, $$\label{four:maximal:def:drift-divergence}
 \frac{|\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(uA_\chi K(w,\cdot))|}{u}
 \le\eta_1\mathcal T+\Pi_N\bigl(|K|^2+a|\nabla K|\bigr).$$ In each of the first three trace stages, $$\label{four:maximal:def:F-derivative}
 w(F)\ge\eta_N a\sigma-\eta_1\mathcal T
   -\Pi_N\bigl(\mathbf1_{\mathcal K}+|K|^2+a|\nabla K|\bigr),$$ where $\mathcal K$ is a fixed compact enlargement of the supports of $C,D_0,D_1$. For fixed $\eta_1$ the bounds remain polynomial in $N$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-def-coefficient-lemma"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-def-coefficient-lemma</summary>

*Proof.* Differentiating $w=l\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f/\sqrt D$ covariantly gives <a id="four:maximal:def:w-derivative-exact"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:def:w-derivative-exact}
 \nabla_iw=A_d(H^f_{i\cdot})+pd\,w\,\partial_i t,
 \qquad
 d\log u=(p+pv+2)dt+H^f(w,\cdot).$$ In the first formula, $d$ is the scalar $D^{-1}$. Relative to the axis, the $A_d$ factor multiplies the axial output of $H^f$ by $d$. The transverse and mixed entries are controlled by <a href="#four:maximal:def:coercivity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:coercivity">[four:maximal:def:coercivity]</a>; the possibly large axial entry occurs as $d(j-K_{ee})$ and is also controlled because $d\le\sqrt d$. Furthermore $d|dt|\le|dt|_{A_d}$. This proves the estimate for $\nabla w$ without an inverse power of $l$ or $d$. For the second formula use $\chi\le d$: the weighted norm of its first term is at most $(2N+2)|dt|_{A_d}$, while its last term is bounded by [(four:maximal:prep:phi-decay)](#four:maximal:prep:phi-decay)$a(|M-K_{e\perp}|+\sqrt\chi\,|j-K_{ee}|)$.

Write $A_\chi=\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}-c(p,v)w\otimes w$, where $c(p,v)=(3+p)/(3+pv)$. The relevant derivatives are $$\partial_pc=\frac{3d}{(3+pv)^2},\qquad
 \partial_vc=-\frac{p(3+p)}{(3+pv)^2},\qquad
 |\nabla v|\le2a|\nabla w|.$$ The $p'$ contribution retains its factor $d$, and is bounded by a polynomial times $d|dt|$. All other terms are bounded by a polynomial times $|\nabla w|$. This proves <a href="#four:maximal:def:derivative-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:derivative-bounds">[four:maximal:def:derivative-bounds]</a>.

In <a href="#four:maximal:def:drift-divergence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:drift-divergence">[four:maximal:def:drift-divergence]</a>, differentiating $u$ contributes at most $$|d\log u|_{A_\chi}|K(w,\cdot)|_{A_\chi}.$$ The other derivatives contribute at most $$|K|(|\nabla A_\chi|+|\nabla w|)+a|\nabla K|.$$ Apply <a href="#four:maximal:def:derivative-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:derivative-bounds">[four:maximal:def:derivative-bounds]</a> and then Young’s inequality to $\Pi_N|K|\sqrt\mathcal T$. Squaring a polynomial remains polynomial, proving <a href="#four:maximal:def:drift-divergence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:drift-divergence">[four:maximal:def:drift-divergence]</a> with the asserted dependence.

For <a href="#four:maximal:def:F-derivative" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:F-derivative">[four:maximal:def:F-derivative]</a>, the common height term gives exactly $w(h)=\eta_N a\sigma$. Derivatives of $C,D_0,D_1$ cost, on $\mathcal K$, a fixed multiple of $1+|\nabla w|$, hence an arbitrarily small fixed multiple of $\mathcal T$ plus a polynomial compact error and $\Pi_N|K|^2$. The only other term is $w(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}K)$ in stage three; it is bounded in absolute value by a fixed multiple of $a|\nabla K|+a|K||\nabla A_\chi|$, handled in the same way. All stage parameters lie in $[0,1]$, so the estimates are uniform in them. This proves the last assertion. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-prop-floor"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:prop:floor" class="proposition">

**Proposition 50** (Floor exclusion). *There is a choice $0<\delta_0<1/4$ independent of $N$ and a positive polynomial $C_N$ such that, for every sufficiently large allowed $R$, no smooth solution of any of the four homotopy stages has $$\min_{\overline{\Omega_R}}t=-\epsilon.$$ These choices use the fixed data and the preceding pointwise and height estimates only. In particular they do not use existence, an upper bound for $Z$, or a uniform Hessian estimate.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-prop-floor"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-prop-floor</summary>

<a id="four:maximal:def:floor-weight-domination"></a>
*Proof.* We first record all end losses that will occur. There is a fixed constant $C_*$ with $$\label{four:maximal:def:floor-weight-domination}
 \mathbf1_{\mathcal K}+|K|^2+vF^2+v|\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g|+a|\nabla K|
 \le C_*(\rho_0+v\rho_1).$$ On a fixed compact set this follows from positivity of $\rho_0$ and Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:height-end" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:height-end">47</a>. Outside that set, $|F|\le |h|+|K|$ in all three trace stages, and the same lemma controls $h^2$ by a fixed multiple of $r^{-2\gamma}$. The metric and tensor decay give $|\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g|=O(r^{-2-q})$, $|K|^2=O(r^{-2-2q})$ and $|\nabla K|=O(r^{-2-q})$. Since $2\gamma<2+q$ and $2+2q>4+\delta$, the curvature and squared tensor terms have the stated bounds. For the derivative term the precise estimate is $$ar^{-2-q}
 \le\tfrac12a^2r^{-2\gamma}
       +\tfrac12r^{-4-2q+2\gamma}
 \le\tfrac12v\rho_1+\tfrac12\rho_0,$$ where $2(q-\gamma)>\delta$ was used. This proves <a href="#four:maximal:def:floor-weight-domination" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:floor-weight-domination">[four:maximal:def:floor-weight-domination]</a>. Also $\rho\le C_\rho\rho_0$ for a fixed $C_\rho$, by its prescribed tail and compact positivity of $\rho_0$.

<a id="four:maximal:def:floor-divergence"></a>
Suppose first that the minimum occurs in the interior in one of the first three stages. Then $dt=0$ and $\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}t\ge0$ there. Proposition <a href="#four:maximal:prop:scalar-identity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:prop:scalar-identity">44</a> and <a href="#four:maximal:def:graph-gauss" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:graph-gauss">[four:maximal:def:graph-gauss]</a> imply, using $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}K=0$, $$u^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}V
 \ge\mu-\tfrac12R_g+J(w)+v\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g(e_f,e_f)
       +\mathcal T-\mathcal S(H^f)+w(F).$$ Here $\mu-R_g/2=-|K|^2/2$ and $|J(w)|\le C_*a|\nabla K|$. Use <a href="#four:maximal:def:floor-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:floor-comparison">[four:maximal:def:floor-comparison]</a>, <a href="#four:maximal:def:F-derivative" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:F-derivative">[four:maximal:def:F-derivative]</a>, and <a href="#four:maximal:def:floor-weight-domination" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:floor-weight-domination">[four:maximal:def:floor-weight-domination]</a>; then pass from $V$ to $V_\lambda=V-(1-\lambda)uA_\chi K(w,\cdot)$ by <a href="#four:maximal:def:drift-divergence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:drift-divergence">[four:maximal:def:drift-divergence]</a>. Choose the two fixed Young errors smaller than $c_2/4$. This yields an absolute $c_3>0$ and a polynomial bound $\Pi_N^{\mathrm f}$ such that at the proposed minimum $$\label{four:maximal:def:floor-divergence}
 u^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}V_\lambda
 \ge c_3\mathcal T+\eta_N a\sigma
       -\Pi_N^{\mathrm f}(\rho_0+v\rho_1).$$ In particular $c_3$ is independent of $N$.

Fix $\delta_0<\min(c_3/2,1/4)$. At the floor $m_0=1$, and the prescribed right side in the first three stages is $\delta_0\mathcal T+\rho+\delta_0\eta_N a\sigma-C_N(\rho_0+v\rho_1)$. The lower bound in <a href="#four:maximal:def:floor-divergence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:floor-divergence">[four:maximal:def:floor-divergence]</a> exceeds it by at least $$(c_3-\delta_0)\mathcal T+(1-\delta_0)\eta_N a\sigma
 +(C_N-\Pi_N^{\mathrm f})(\rho_0+v\rho_1)-\rho.$$ Choose $C_N\ge\Pi_N^{\mathrm f}+C_\rho+1$. The last display is strictly positive because $\rho_0>0$, contradicting the equation. This choice is polynomial and independent of $R$ and of the solution.

In stage four use <a href="#four:maximal:def:terminal-reduction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:terminal-reduction">[four:maximal:def:terminal-reduction]</a>. At an interior floor minimum the left side is $u^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(3u\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}t)=3\Delta t\ge0$, while the right side is $$\eta\bigl(\delta_0|K|^2/2+\rho-C_N\rho_0\bigr).$$ Increasing $C_N$ by a fixed constant makes the bracket strictly negative everywhere, since $|K|^2\le C_*\rho_0$. Thus an interior floor minimum is impossible whenever $\eta>0$.

An inner boundary minimum in the first three stages is also impossible. At $t=-\epsilon$ we have $j_0=0$. Since $V_\lambda=V-(1-\lambda)uA_\chi K(w,\cdot)$, the drift correction in <a href="#four:maximal:def:homotopy-boundary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:homotopy-boundary">[four:maximal:def:homotopy-boundary]</a> cancels, leaving $V_\nu/u=\mathcal B$. Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:boundary-identity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:boundary-identity">46</a> therefore gives $$3\partial_\nu t=-H-N_B<0.$$ This contradicts the nonnegative derivative into $\Omega_R$ required at a boundary minimum. In stage four, where $f=0$, the corresponding formula is $3\partial_\nu t=\eta(-H-N_B)<0$ for $\eta>0$. The outer boundary is excluded by Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:height-end" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:height-end">47</a>.

It remains to consider $\eta=0$. The last-stage equation and boundary conditions then reduce to $$\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(3L_0(Z)\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Z)=0,\qquad
 \partial_\nu Z|_B=0,\qquad Z|_{S_R}=0.$$ Multiplying by $Z$ and integrating gives $\int_{\Omega_R}3L_0(Z)|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Z|^2\,\mathrm dV_g=0$. Thus $Z=t=0$, which is strictly above the floor. This treats every stage and every possible location of a floor minimum. ◻

</details>

The order of the choices is now fixed: strict background data and collars, $\epsilon$ and the cutoffs, the absolute small $\delta_0$, the polynomial $C_N$, and finally sufficiently large $N$ and allowed $R$. The estimates in the next Section concern arbitrary smooth admissible solutions with $t\ge-\epsilon$. Proposition <a href="#four:maximal:prop:floor" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:prop:floor">50</a> separately ensures that a homotopy solution cannot meet the boundary of this range.

<a id="four:maximal:sec:bounds"></a>
### Global a priori bounds

Throughout this section the strict background data, collars, and $\epsilon>0$ are fixed. We consider arbitrary smooth solutions of the homotopy on $\Omega_R$ satisfying $t\ge-\epsilon$. Existence is not assumed: each assertion is an estimate for every solution that might occur. The constants denoted by $\Pi_N$ are bounded by a polynomial in $N$, independently of the solution, homotopy parameter, and allowed radius. Constants denoted by $C(N)$ may depend arbitrarily on the fixed integer $N$. All integrals without an indicated graph measure use $g$.

<a id="pm-h-61"></a>
#### Separation from the threshold region

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-lem-separation"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:lem:separation" class="lemma">

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:separation"></a>
**Lemma 51** (Compact separation). *Let $Q_0$ be a compact subset of $\overline\Omega$ disjoint from $\mathcal D_c$. There are $\eta_2>0$, $N_0$, and allowed radii $R_{\min}(N)\to\infty$ such that, in stages 1 and 2, $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:separation}
 h\ge c+\eta_2\quad\hbox{on }Q_0
 \qquad(N\ge N_0,\ R\ge R_{\min}(N)).$$ The constants are uniform over both stages.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-lem-separation"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-lem-separation</summary>

*Proof.* We first identify the geometric inequality satisfied by a relaxed limit. Take any sequence of admissible solutions with $N_i\to\infty$ and allowed $R_i\to\infty$, and write $$\underline h(x)=\lim_{j\to\infty}
 \inf\{h_i(y):i\ge j,\ \mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(x,y)<j^{-1}\}.$$ On compact sets this is a finite lower semicontinuous function, by Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:height-end" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:height-end">47</a>. Let a smooth function $\phi$ touch $\underline h$ from below at an interior point $x$, with $\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}\phi(x)\ne0$. Subtracting a small multiple of the fourth power of the distance makes the contact strict without changing its two-jet. Minimization on a small closed ball then gives a subsequence of local lower contacts of $\phi$ plus constants with $h_i$, at points $x_i\to x$, whose contact values converge to $\underline h(x)$.

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:lower-test"></a>
At these contacts, $\eta_{N_i}\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f_i=\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}\phi$, so $$l_i\sigma_i\ge\frac{\ell_i}{\eta_{N_i}}|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}\phi(x_i)|\longrightarrow\infty,
 \qquad d_i,\chi_i\longrightarrow0,\quad a_i\longrightarrow1.$$ In particular this conclusion uses the floor and the fixed test gradient, rather than an estimate for the solution gradients. Put $\nu_\phi=\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}\phi/|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}\phi|$. Positivity of $A_\chi$ and the Hessian inequality at a lower contact give $$\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_{\chi_i}}K+
 \frac{a_i}{|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}\phi|}
       \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_{\chi_i}}\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}\phi
 \le F_i\le h_i.$$ The last inequality holds throughout stages 1 and 2 because $C\le0$ and $D_0\le0$. Passing to the limit proves $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:lower-test}
 \frac{\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{\nu_\phi^\perp}\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}\phi}{|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}\phi|}
       +\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{\nu_\phi^\perp}K\le\underline h(x).$$ The left side is the outward expansion of the regular level of $\phi$. Neither convergence of the homotopy parameters nor continuity bounds for the solution coefficients were needed.

Fix $c<k<k'<0$. Apply Lemma <a href="#n3:apriori:sublevel-support" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:apriori:sublevel-support">21</a> on $U=\operatorname{int}\Omega$ with $u=\underline h$, $Q=K$ and $q_0=k'$. The relaxed limit is finite and lower semicontinuous. At a nonzero-gradient lower test whose contact value is less than $k'$, <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:lower-test" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:lower-test">[four:maximal:bounds:lower-test]</a> bounds its expansion by that value, hence by $k'$. The lemma therefore shows that every smooth exterior support to the closed sublevel $\{\underline h\le k\}$ at an interior frontier point has expansion at most $k'$. In particular, this conclusion also applies when the sublevel has a plateau at height $k$.

Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:height-end" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:height-end">47</a> makes this sublevel bounded: for a large fixed $r$, its lower height bound exceeds the fixed negative number $k$. Adjoin $\mathcal D_c$ to obtain a compact closed set. At a frontier point on $B$, each exterior support also supports $\mathcal D_c$; tangency comparison with its smooth boundary gives expansion at most $c$. Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:support-enclosure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:support-enclosure">43</a> therefore places the union in $\mathcal D_{c'}$ for every $k'<c'<0$.

Hausdorff right continuity at $c$ and the positive distance of $Q_0$ from $\mathcal D_c$ allow us to choose $c<k<k'<c'<0$ so that $\mathcal D_{c'}\cap Q_0=\varnothing$. If <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:separation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:separation">[four:maximal:bounds:separation]</a> failed, choose $N_i\to\infty$, allowed $R_i\ge i$, and $x_i\in Q_0$ with $h_i(x_i)\le c+i^{-1}$. A subsequence has $x_i\to x\in Q_0$, and then $\underline h(x)\le c<k$, contradicting that containment. This also proves uniformity over the two stages. Enlarging the allowed radius function never invalidates the assertion. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-62"></a>
#### Collar barriers and polynomial trace estimates

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-lem-collar-slopes"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:lem:collar-slopes" class="lemma">

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:collar-slopes"></a>
**Lemma 52** (Inner collar slopes). *For all sufficiently large $N$ and allowed $R$, there are fixed constants $0<c_5<C_6$ such that $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:collar-slopes}
 \frac{c_5}{\eta_N}\le\partial_\nu f\le\frac{C_6}{\eta_N}
 \quad\hbox{in stages 1 and 2},\qquad
 |\partial_\nu f|\le\frac{C_6}{\eta_N}
 \quad\hbox{in stage 3}.$$ Here $\nu$ points into $\Omega$. In stage 4, $f=0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-lem-collar-slopes"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-lem-collar-slopes</summary>

*Proof.* Use a fixed short collar $0\le s\le s_0$ from Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:threshold-collars" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:threshold-collars">42</a>, with $C=-\kappa s$, $\nu_s=\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}s/|\,\mathrm ds|$, and $0<c_s\le|\,\mathrm ds|\le C_s$. All its geometric derivatives are bounded, and $P_s+H_s\ge c$, where $P_s=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{\{s=\mathrm{constant}\}}K$. The finitely many outer collar faces satisfy Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:separation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:separation">51</a>.

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:collar-operator"></a>
For a positive-slope test $h_0=c+\psi(s)$, the trace operator, with $t$ computed from the solution’s $Z$ and the common contact gradient, is exactly $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:collar-operator}
 P_s+aH_s+\chi K(\nu_s,\nu_s)
 +a\chi\left(
    \frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}s(\nu_s,\nu_s)}{|\,\mathrm ds|}
       +|\,\mathrm ds|\frac{\psi''}{\psi'}\right).$$ For a test with negative slope, replace $a$ by $-a$ in this formula. If $|\psi'|$ lies between fixed positive constants, the floor gives <a id="four:maximal:bounds:steep-coefficients"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:bounds:steep-coefficients}
 d\le C(\eta_N/\ell)^2=Ce^{-\epsilon N},\qquad
 1-a\le d,\qquad
 \frac{N\chi}{d}=\frac{3N}{3+pv}\ge\frac{3N}{3+N}.$$ Thus $a\ge1/2$ and $N\chi\ge c_4d$ for large $N$.

Choose a fixed smooth $\vartheta_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ equal to one on $[0,1]$ and zero on $[2,\infty)$, and put $b_N(s)=\Lambda_* N\vartheta_1(Ns)$, where $\Lambda_*>0$ is a fixed collar constant, independent of $N$. The constant will be chosen large; its crucial property is $$0\le\int_0^{s_0}b_N(s)\,\mathrm ds\le2\Lambda_*.$$ For the lower barrier in stages 1 and 2, prescribe $\psi'(s)=q_-\exp(\int_0^s b_N)$ and $\psi(0)=0$. For the chosen value of $\Lambda_*$, take $q_->0$ so small that $\psi'\le\kappa/2$ and $\psi(s_0)<\eta_2$. Positive normal direction makes $D_0=0$. Subtracting the prescribed trace right side from <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:collar-operator" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:collar-operator">[four:maximal:bounds:collar-operator]</a> gives a residual at least <a id="four:maximal:bounds:lower-residual"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:bounds:lower-residual}
 \kappa s/2-Cd+a\chi|\,\mathrm ds|b_N(s).$$ The constant $C$ in this residual depends only on collar geometry. We choose $\Lambda_*$ so large that the last term dominates $2Cd$ on $[0,1/N]$. On $[1/N,s_0]$, the first term dominates $Cd$ for large $N$, because $Ne^{-\epsilon N}\to0$, and the last term has a favorable sign. This is a strict lower barrier. Its outer value is below $h$ by separation and its inner value agrees with $h$.

For the upper barrier take $\psi'(s)=q_+\exp(-\int_0^s b_N)$. Choose its fixed minimum slope larger than twice the bounded linear variation of $P_s+H_s-c+\kappa s$, and choose $q_+$ still larger if needed to dominate the height bound at $s_0$. The residual is now at most $-c_7s+Cd-a\chi|\,\mathrm ds|b_N$, for fixed $c_7>0$. The same two intervals prove strict negativity. The bounded integral of $b_N$ leaves all lower and upper test slopes between fixed positive constants, independently of $N$.

For completeness, at an interior positive maximum of $h_0-h$, the test Hessian is at most the solution Hessian, whereas its height is larger. The positive principal matrix and the strictly increasing dependence of $F$ on $h$ contradict a positive test residual. This proves lower comparison; reversing the difference proves upper comparison. In both comparisons $Z$ and the gradient are the same at contact, so all coefficients other than the height agree. Taking inward derivatives at $s=0$ gives the first assertion of <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:collar-slopes" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:collar-slopes">[four:maximal:bounds:collar-slopes]</a>.

In stage 3 the face height is $b_\zeta=(1-\zeta)c$. Use $b_\zeta\pm\psi(s)$ with fixed large positive slopes and $\psi''/\psi'=-b_N$. At $s=0$ the two unit-direction inequalities in <a href="#four:maximal:def:face-direction-signs" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:face-direction-signs">[four:maximal:def:face-direction-signs]</a> say that the positive-slope residual is nonpositive and the negative-slope residual is nonnegative. Replacing $\pm \nu_s$ by $\pm a\nu_s$ costs $O(d)$, including the term $\chi K(\nu_s,\nu_s)$; moving to distance $s$ costs $O(s)$, uniformly in $\zeta$. The change of height then supplies a strict linear margin, with the desired sign, when the minimum test slope exceeds the fixed spatial error constant. The term involving $b_N$ has the correct sign for both tests and dominates the $O(d)$ error on $[0,1/N]$. On the remainder the linear margin dominates it. The height bound handles $s=s_0$. These two comparisons bound the slope in absolute value in stage 3. The terminal trace equation has $f=0$, as established in Section <a href="#four:maximal:sec:deformation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:sec:deformation">12</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-lem-weighted-trace"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:lem:weighted-trace" class="lemma">

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:bounds:boundary-absorption"></a>
**Lemma 53** (Weighted trace and boundary flux). *Let $\mathcal C$ be a fixed union of collars. In stages 1 and 2, every nonnegative $C^1$ function $\varphi$ satisfies $$\begin{aligned}
 \int_B L_0\varphi
 &\le\Pi_N\int_{\mathcal C}
  u\bigl((1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})\varphi+|\,\mathrm d\varphi|_{A_\chi}\bigr),
       \label{four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted}\\
 \int_B\varphi
 &\le\Pi_N\int_{\mathcal C}
  \sqrt D\bigl((1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})\varphi+|\,\mathrm d\varphi|_{A_\chi}\bigr).
       \label{four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted}
\end{aligned}$$ The integrands vanish outside the support of $\varphi$ and its derivative; thus both statements localize to any base patch. Moreover $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux}
 |(V_\lambda)_\nu|\le C_7ud=C_7L_0\sqrt d
                     \le C_8(\eta_N/\ell)L_0.$$ Consequently, $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:boundary-absorption}
 \int_B|(V_\lambda)_\nu|
 \le \Pi_N\frac{\eta_N}{\ell}
             \int_{\mathcal C}u(\rho+\delta_0\mathcal T).$$ All constants in these assertions have the stated polynomial control.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-lem-weighted-trace"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-lem-weighted-trace</summary>

*Proof.* Set $W=l\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}_{\bar g}f=\sqrt d\,w$. For each covector $\xi$, $$|\xi(W)|\le|\xi|_{A_d}
       \le\sqrt{(3+N)/3}\,|\xi|_{A_\chi},\qquad uW=L_0w.$$ The second inequality follows from $d/\chi=(3+pv)/3$. Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:collar-slopes" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:collar-slopes">52</a> gives $w\cdot\nu=a\ge1/2$ on $B$. Direct differentiation yields $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathop{\mathrm{div}}w&=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_d}H^f+dp\,w(t),\\
 u^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(uW)
 &=\sqrt d\bigl(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_d}H^f+(dp+p+2)w(t)\bigr),\\
 D^{-1/2}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(\sqrt D W)
 &=\sqrt d\bigl(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_d}H^f+dp\,w(t)\bigr).
\end{aligned}$$ These last two expressions have absolute value at most $\Pi_N(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})$ on the collars. Indeed the axial tensor term is $d^{3/2}H^f_{ee}$, controlled by [(four:maximal:def:coercivity)](#four:maximal:def:coercivity) the $d j^2$ term of Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:coercivity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:coercivity">45</a>, and $\sqrt d\,|w(t)|\le|\,\mathrm dt|_{A_d}$; all background $K$ terms are bounded there. No inverse power of $l$ has occurred.

Take a fixed collar cutoff $\eta$, equal to one near $B$ and zero near the outer collar faces. Apply the divergence theorem to $\eta\varphi uW$. The domain’s outward normal on $B$ is $-\nu$, so the boundary integral is $-\int_B L_0a\varphi$. Taking absolute values of the three interior terms, and using $a\ge1/2$, proves <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted">[four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted]</a>. The derivative of $\eta$ costs only a fixed multiple of $\varphi$. Using $\sqrt D W=w$ instead proves <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted">[four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted]</a>. The same computation proves the asserted localization.

On $B$, positive slope gives $w_\nu=a$, $D_0=0$, and $F=c=P_B+H$. Thus the expression inside the boundary multiplier of the homotopy is $$(a-1)H-N_Bd-(1-\lambda)\chi aK(\nu,\nu).$$ The multiplier lies in $[0,1]$, and $1-a\le d$, $\chi\le d$. This proves the first inequality in <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux">[four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux]</a>. The lower collar slope gives $\sqrt d\le(l|\partial_\nu f|)^{-1}\le C\eta_N/\ell$, proving the rest. Finally apply <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted">[four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted]</a> with $\varphi=1$. On the fixed collars, $\rho$ has a positive minimum, so $1+\sqrt{\mathcal T}\le C(\rho+\delta_0\mathcal T)$ with fixed $C$. This proves <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:boundary-absorption" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:boundary-absorption">[four:maximal:bounds:boundary-absorption]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-63"></a>
#### The global high-level energy bound

The collar estimates have already made the inner flux small with polynomial constants. We now obtain a bounded range for the conformal variable at each fixed parameter. That is a separate task: its constants may be arbitrary at fixed parameter because the mass estimate will return to the earlier collar bounds.

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:high-source"></a>
We now allow arbitrary constants $C(N)$. At sufficiently high levels $Z>Z_0(N)>0$, the unscaled source satisfies $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:high-source}
 \Xi\ge\delta_0\mathcal T+\rho+\tfrac12\delta_0\eta_N a\sigma.$$ To see this, $\mathcal P$ is bounded at fixed $N$, and on the admissible support of $m_0$ we have $-\epsilon\le t\le-\epsilon+1/N$. There $D=e^{6(Z-t)}$ and $\eta_N a\sigma=(\eta_N/l)(\sqrt D-D^{-1/2})$ tends uniformly to infinity as $Z\to\infty$. Outside this band the penalty vanishes. On the full range we also have $\Xi\ge\delta_0\mathcal T-C(N)$.

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:global-energy"></a>
Only stage 1 requires an energy argument to handle its nonzero drift. Choose a smooth nondecreasing $k_0$ which is zero below $Z_0$, one above $Z_0+1$, and has bounded derivative. Testing the divergence equation with $k_0(Z)$, whose outer trace is zero, gives $$\int_{\Omega_R}uk_0\Xi
       +3\int_{\Omega_R}uk_0'|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}^2
 =-\int_B k_0(V_\lambda)_\nu
       -\lambda\int_{\Omega_R}uk_0'
                   \langle K(w,\cdot),\,\mathrm dZ\rangle_{A_\chi}.$$ Young’s inequality absorbs half the gradient term and leaves $C\int uk_0'|K|^2$. This is at most $C(N)$: on the derivative strip, $$u=l e^{3Z-t}\le e^{1+3(Z_0+1)+\epsilon},$$ and $|K|^2$ is integrable since $q>1$. By <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux">[four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux]</a> and <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted">[four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted]</a>, the boundary cost is at most $$\Pi_N\frac{\eta_N}{\ell}\int_{\mathcal C}
   u\bigl((1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})k_0+k_0'|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}\bigr).$$ The first term is absorbed by a fixed fraction of $\int uk_0(\delta_0\mathcal T+\rho)$ for large $N$, because $\Pi_N\eta_N/\ell\to0$. Young’s inequality absorbs the second term into $\int uk_0'|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}^2$ and a bounded derivative-strip integral over $\mathcal C$. We obtain $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:global-energy}
 \int_{\Omega_R}u\bigl[
       k_0(\mathcal T+\rho+\eta_N a\sigma)
                    +k_0'|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}^2\bigr]\le C(N).$$ This is uniform in $R$ and in the stage 1 parameter.

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:graph-comparison"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:bounds:graph-l2"></a>
Let $\Gamma$ denote the ordinary graph of $f$ in $(\Omega,g)\times\mathbb R$ with product metric $g+\,\mathrm db^2$. This is a four-dimensional graph. Its measure and gradient satisfy, at fixed $N$, $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:graph-comparison}
 \,\mathrm d\Gamma\asymp_N\sqrt D\,\mathrm dV_g,\qquad
 |\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}_\Gamma\phi|\asymp_N|\,\mathrm d\phi|_{A_\chi}.$$ These comparisons use only $\ell\le l\le e$ and $3d/(3+N)\le\chi\le d$. Also $$D^{1/3}\le C(N)(1+\eta_N a\sigma),\qquad
 e^{2Z}\sqrt D=l^{-1}uD^{1/3}.$$ For the first inequality, put $y=l\sigma$. It is immediate for $y\le1$; for $y\ge1$ use $\eta_N a\sigma\ge(\eta_N/(\sqrt2 l))y$ and $y^{2/3}\le y$. On any fixed compact base set $Q$, the positive minimum of $\rho$ and <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:global-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:global-energy">[four:maximal:bounds:global-energy]</a> control the integral of $u(1+\eta_N a\sigma)$ above $Z_0+1$. Below that level the floor and $D=e^{6(Z-t)}$ bound every integrand on $Q$. Consequently $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:graph-l2}
 \int_{\Gamma\cap\pi^{-1}(Q)} e^{2Z}\,\mathrm d\Gamma\le C(N,Q).$$ Here $\pi$ is the graph projection. The estimate is local in the base; the global estimate from which it follows is <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:global-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:global-energy">[four:maximal:bounds:global-energy]</a>.

<a id="pm-h-64"></a>
#### Graph Sobolev inequality and the exponential test

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:graph-sobolev"></a>
We continue with stage 1 for the next two estimates. For a fixed compact base patch and a function $\omega$ supported over it, away from $S_R$ but possibly meeting $B$, we claim $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:graph-sobolev}
 \|\omega\|_{L^4(\,\mathrm d\Gamma)}^2
 \le C(N)\int_\Gamma
       \bigl(|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}_\Gamma\omega|^2+(1+\mathcal T)\omega^2\bigr)\,\mathrm d\Gamma.$$ Extend a compact enlargement of the base metric smoothly to a closed manifold and use a smooth isometric Euclidean embedding (Nash 1956, Theorem 2, p. 59) <a id="pm-cite-60"></a>[[Nash1956](#ref-Nash1956)]. Its product with $\mathbb R$ gives a Euclidean immersion of the graph. The contribution to its mean curvature from the base embedding is bounded by a fixed constant: it is a trace of the fixed second fundamental form on a four-dimensional tangent plane. The remaining product mean curvature has magnitude $$\frac{\sqrt D}{l\sqrt{1+\sigma^2}}
 \left|\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\perp H^f+(1+\sigma^2)^{-1}H^f_{ee}\right|
 \le C(N)(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T}).$$ Indeed the prefactor is bounded at fixed $N$, while $(1+\sigma^2)^{-1}\le C(N)d$ and the axial term is controlled by $d j^2$ in Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:coercivity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:coercivity">45</a>.

The Euclidean submanifold Sobolev inequality in dimension four gives $$\left(\int_\Gamma |\omega|^4\,\mathrm d\Gamma\right)^{3/4}
 \le C(N)\int_\Gamma
    \bigl(|\omega|^2|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}_\Gamma\omega|
               +(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})|\omega|^3\bigr)\,\mathrm d\Gamma
           +C\int_B|\omega|^3.$$ We have applied the $L^1$ Sobolev inequality to $|\omega|^3$; see Michael–Simon (Michael and Simon 1973) <a id="pm-cite-61"></a>[[MichaelSimon1973](#ref-MichaelSimon1973)] and the precise rectifiable-submanifold statement in (Simon 2014, chap. 4, §5, Theorem 5.7, p. 98) <a id="pm-cite-62"></a>[[Simon2014](#ref-Simon2014)]. Its hypotheses hold for this smooth multiplicity-one immersion with locally integrable mean curvature and compactly supported test. To justify the displayed boundary term from the interior statement, extend each individual smooth graph across $B$ and cut off in an exterior strip whose width tends to zero. The integral of the cutoff gradient tends to the boundary integral, while the strip’s other integrals tend to zero. This requires smoothness of each graph, not a uniform curvature estimate for extensions. The induced boundary metric is $g|_B$, since $f$ is constant there.

Apply <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted">[four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted]</a> to $|\omega|^3$ and then <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:graph-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:graph-comparison">[four:maximal:bounds:graph-comparison]</a>. It bounds the last term by the same two interior terms. Each such term is at most $$C(N)\left(\int_\Gamma|\omega|^4\,\mathrm d\Gamma\right)^{1/2}
 \left(\int_\Gamma
       (|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}_\Gamma\omega|^2+(1+\mathcal T)\omega^2)\,\mathrm d\Gamma\right)^{1/2}$$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Dividing, and squaring, proves <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:graph-sobolev" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:graph-sobolev">[four:maximal:bounds:graph-sobolev]</a>; the case $\omega=0$ is immediate.

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:exponential-energy"></a>
Next let $\psi$ be a smooth compact base cutoff of the same kind. There is $k_*(N)\ge1$ such that for every real $k\ge k_*(N)$, $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:exponential-energy}
 \int_\Gamma e^{2kZ}\psi^2
        (\mathcal T+k|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}_\Gamma Z|^2)\,\mathrm d\Gamma
 \le C(N)k\int_\Gamma e^{2kZ}
               (\psi^2+|\,\mathrm d\psi|_g^2)\,\mathrm d\Gamma.$$ The constant $C(N)$ here is independent of $k$. To prove this, test the stage 1 divergence equation with $\varphi=\psi^2e^{2kZ}/L_0$. Write $Q=\psi^2e^{2kZ}$ and $b=\lambda K(w,\cdot)$. After integration, cancellation of $L_0$ gives the exact identity $$\begin{aligned}
 &\int_{\Omega_R}\sqrt D\,Q
       \bigl(\Xi+6k|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}^2\bigr)\\
 &=-\int_B(V_\lambda)_\nu Q/L_0
   -\int_{\Omega_R}\sqrt D\,e^{2kZ}
       \bigl[2\psi\langle3\,\mathrm dZ+b,\,\mathrm d\psi\rangle_{A_\chi}
          +2k\psi^2\langle b,\,\mathrm dZ\rangle_{A_\chi}\bigr]\\
 &\hspace{1cm}
   +\int_{\Omega_R}\sqrt D\,Q(p+2)
                    \langle3\,\mathrm dZ+b,\,\mathrm dt\rangle_{A_\chi}.
\end{aligned}$$ Use $\Xi\ge\delta_0\mathcal T-C(N)$, $|b|_{A_\chi}\le|K|$, and Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:coercivity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:coercivity">45</a>. For example, $$(p+2)|\,\mathrm dt|_{A_\chi}(|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}+|K|)
 \le\frac{\delta_0}{8}\mathcal T
               +C(N)(|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}^2+|K|^2).$$ Young’s inequality handles the drift and cutoff products with a fixed fraction of $k|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}^2$ and a remainder bounded by $C(N)k e^{2kZ}(\psi^2+|\,\mathrm d\psi|^2)$. Choose $k_*(N)$ large enough to absorb the preceding $C(N)|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}^2$ term.

By <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux">[four:maximal:bounds:boundary-flux]</a> the boundary contribution is at most $C\int_B Q$ (enlarging a fixed constant since $\eta_N/\ell\le1$). Applying <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted">[four:maximal:bounds:trace-unweighted]</a> to $Q$ gives, only on $\mathcal C\cap\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\psi$, $$C(N)\int\sqrt D\,e^{2kZ}
   \bigl[(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})\psi^2
       +2|\psi||\,\mathrm d\psi|+2k\psi^2|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}\bigr].$$ The $\sqrt{\mathcal T}$ and $k|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}$ terms are absorbed by small fixed fractions of $\delta_0\psi^2\mathcal T$ and $k\psi^2|\,\mathrm dZ|_{A_\chi}^2$, leaving at most $C(N)k e^{2kZ}(\psi^2+|\,\mathrm d\psi|^2)$. Finally <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:graph-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:graph-comparison">[four:maximal:bounds:graph-comparison]</a> proves <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:exponential-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:exponential-energy">[four:maximal:bounds:exponential-energy]</a>. In particular, neither the trace cutoff nor differentiation of $1/L_0$ introduces a constant exponential in $k$.

<a id="pm-h-65"></a>
#### Moser iteration and the full range

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-prop-bounded-range"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:prop:bounded-range" class="proposition">

<a id="four:maximal:bounds:bounded-range"></a>
**Proposition 54** (Bounded variables). *For every sufficiently large fixed $N$ and all sufficiently large allowed $R$, every admissible smooth homotopy solution satisfies $$\label{four:maximal:bounds:bounded-range}
 |f|\le C_0/\eta_N,\qquad
 -\epsilon\le t\le Z\le C(N),\qquad |\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f|\le C(N).$$ The constants are independent of $R$, the solution, and the homotopy parameter. No uniform Hessian or coefficient continuity estimate is used in obtaining these bounds.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-prop-bounded-range"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-prop-bounded-range</summary>

*Proof.* We first finish stage 1. Apply <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:graph-sobolev" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:graph-sobolev">[four:maximal:bounds:graph-sobolev]</a> to $\omega=\psi e^{kZ}$ and then use <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:exponential-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:exponential-energy">[four:maximal:bounds:exponential-energy]</a>. If $\psi=1$ on a smaller patch and $|\,\mathrm d\psi|\le C/\mathrm{gap}$, the resulting norm step is $$\|e^Z\|_{L^{4k}(\text{smaller graph})}
 \le\bigl[C(N)k^2(1+\mathrm{gap}^{-2})\bigr]^{1/(2k)}
       \|e^Z\|_{L^{2k}(\text{larger graph})}.$$ Choose $k_j=2^j k_*(N)$ and geometrically decreasing gaps between fixed nested base patches. The logarithms of the factors sum because $\sum_j (1+j)/2^j<\infty$. Writing $S(r)=\sup_{Q_r}e^Z$ for a nested family of compact patches gives $$S(r')\le C(N)(r''-r')^{-A(N)}
          \|e^Z\|_{L^{2k_*}(\Gamma\cap\pi^{-1}(Q_{r''}))}.$$ Interpolation with <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:graph-l2" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:graph-l2">[four:maximal:bounds:graph-l2]</a> yields $$\|e^Z\|_{2k_*}
     \le S(r'')^{1-1/k_*}\|e^Z\|_2^{1/k_*}.$$ If $k_*=1$ this already proves the bound. Otherwise Young’s inequality gives, for every $\alpha>0$, $$S(r')\le\alpha S(r'')
       +C(N,\alpha)(r''-r')^{-A'(N)}.$$ Iterate over radii increasing geometrically to a fixed larger radius and take $\alpha<2^{-A'(N)-1}$. The sum of the remainder terms is finite. The final term $\alpha^j S(r_j)$ tends to zero for each individual smooth solution, since all $Q_{r_j}$ lie in a fixed compact patch. The resulting bound is independent of that individual supremum. Finitely many such patches prove an upper bound for $Z$ on any fixed compact base set, including $B$.

To extend the bound along the end, use <a href="#four:maximal:def:drift-divergence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:def:drift-divergence">[four:maximal:def:drift-divergence]</a>, with a fixed small coefficient: $$u^{-1}|\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(uA_\chi K(w,\cdot))|
 \le\frac{\delta_0}{4}\mathcal T
       +\Pi_N(|K|^2+a|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}K|).$$ Since $a\sigma= l\sigma^2/\sqrt D\ge e^{-1}a^2$, Young’s inequality bounds the second term by $$\frac{\delta_0}{4}\eta_N a\sigma
       +C(N)(|K|^2+|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}K|^2).$$ The last expression, apart from its favorable term, is $o(\rho)$ on the end. Indeed $2+2q>4+\delta$ and $|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}K|^2=O(r^{-4-2q})$. Beyond a sufficiently large fixed-$N$ sphere, the high-level source <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:high-source" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:high-source">[four:maximal:bounds:high-source]</a> therefore implies $$\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(3uA_\chi\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Z)>0
 \quad\hbox{where }Z>Z_0(N).$$ At an interior maximum its left side is $3uA_\chi:\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}Z\le0$, a contradiction. The compact bound controls the inner sphere and $Z=0$ on $S_R$. This proves the global upper bound in stage 1.

In stages 2 and 3, $\lambda=0$. The same high-level source is strictly positive, so it excludes interior high maxima directly. The boundary slope bound implies $$Z=t+\tfrac16\log(1+l^2|\partial_\nu f|^2)
       \le t+\tfrac16\log(1+e^2 C_6^2/\eta_N^2)
       \quad\hbox{on }B.$$ Thus sufficiently high boundary $Z$ forces $t\ge1$. At such points $j_0(t)=1$, and the boundary prescription gives zero conormal flux. The boundary point principle excludes a nonconstant high maximum there: in a neighborhood of the maximum the individual smooth operator is elliptic and $\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(3uA_\chi\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Z)>0$, so its outward conormal derivative at a boundary maximum is strictly positive, contrary to the zero datum. This uses ellipticity only for each individual solution. The outer Dirichlet value is zero, so the upper bound follows uniformly through these stages.

In stage 4, $f=0$ and $t=Z$. For positive scaling $\eta$, sufficiently high levels lie outside the penalty band and have source $\eta(\delta_0\mathcal T+\rho)>0$; the same maximum and boundary point argument applies. At zero scaling, multiplying the homogeneous equation by $Z$ gives $\int 3L_0|\,\mathrm dZ|^2=0$, and the outer value yields $Z=0$. These bounds are uniform even as $\eta\downarrow0$.

Finally the height bound is Lemma <a href="#four:maximal:lem:height-end" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:lem:height-end">47</a>, and $t\le Z$ follows from $D\ge1$. The implicit equation gives $$D=e^{6(Z-t)}\le e^{6(C(N)+\epsilon)},\qquad
 |\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f|^2=(D-1)/l^2\le\ell^{-2}e^{6(C(N)+\epsilon)}.$$ This proves <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:bounded-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:bounded-range">[four:maximal:bounds:bounded-range]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-bounds-parameter-order"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:bounds:parameter-order" class="remark">

*Remark 55*. Separation, the collar slopes, and <a href="#four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted">[four:maximal:bounds:trace-weighted]</a>–<a href="#four:maximal:bounds:boundary-absorption" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:bounds:boundary-absorption">[four:maximal:bounds:boundary-absorption]</a> were proved before introducing any arbitrary $C(N)$. The graph comparisons, Moser iteration, and subsequent regularity may have arbitrary fixed-$N$ losses. The final mass comparison uses the earlier weighted trace and boundary-flux inequalities directly; none of these later constants enters its limit as $N\to\infty$.

</div>

<a id="four:maximal:sec:regularity"></a>
### Local regularity of the coupled system

The bounded-range estimate makes the trace equation uniformly elliptic at fixed $N$. The second equation still contains $|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Z|^2$ and $|\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f|^2$, so classical estimates cannot yet be applied to it. We first use Theorem [four:thm:axial-regularity] [four:thm:axial-regularity](#four:thm:axial-regularity) to control $df$ and the local integral of $|\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f|^2$. The scalar measure-source estimate of Lemma <a href="#b:lem:natural-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="b:lem:natural-growth">28</a> then gives Hölder continuity of $Z$, including at both boundary types. These two gains start the classical bootstrap.

All constants in this section may depend arbitrarily on the fixed data and $N$. The earlier polynomial bounds will control the final energy error. In coordinate calculations $D$ denotes ordinary differentiation; the graph scalar $D=1+l^2|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f|^2$ retains its earlier meaning in geometric formulas.

<a id="stmt-four-maximal-prop-classical-estimates"></a>
<div id="four:maximal:prop:classical-estimates" class="proposition">

**Proposition 56**. *Fix the strict data, $\epsilon$, a sufficiently large $N$, and any of the homotopy stages of Section <a href="#four:maximal:sec:deformation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:sec:deformation">12</a>. Every smooth solution on an allowed finite truncation with $t\ge-\epsilon$ has uniform local bounds for every finite number of derivatives of $f$ and $Z$, including up to the inner and outer boundary faces. On the uniform unit patches on the end these constants are independent of the outer truncation radius and of the stage parameter. They may depend arbitrarily on $N$. In particular, on a fixed finite truncation they bound the $C^{1,\alpha}$ norm of $Z$ for each fixed $0<\alpha<1$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-maximal-prop-classical-estimates"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-maximal-prop-classical-estimates</summary>

*Proof.* Work on the uniform interior and boundary-normal patches of the prepared geometry.

<a id="pm-h-67"></a>
###### The axial estimate and the Hessian measure.

<a id="four:maximal:reg:f-normalized"></a>
<a id="four:maximal:reg:f-hessian-measure"></a>
Proposition <a href="#four:maximal:prop:bounded-range" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:maximal:prop:bounded-range">54</a> bounds $f,Z,t,\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f$ and keeps $l/\sqrt D$ bounded above and away from zero at fixed $N$. Dividing the trace equation by this factor gives $$\label{four:maximal:reg:f-normalized}
 A_\chi:\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f=G_f,\qquad
 G_f=\frac{\sqrt D}{l}
             \bigl(F-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}K\bigr),\qquad
 |G_f|\le C(N),\quad \chi\ge\chi _0(N)>0.$$ The geometry of each patch has the bounds required by Theorem [four:thm:axial-regularity] [four:thm:axial-regularity](#four:thm:axial-regularity), and each face value of $f$ is constant. Each individual solution is smooth; the theorem’s constants depend only on the bounded gradient, source, geometry and ellipticity. It gives a uniform Hölder bound for $\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f$ and $$\label{four:maximal:reg:f-hessian-measure}
 \int_{B_r(x)\cap\Omega_R}|\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f|^2\,\mathrm dV_g
                              \le C(N)r^{2+2\alpha}.$$ Coordinate Hessians satisfy the same estimate, since their difference from covariant Hessians is bounded. At a face the theorem uses the $C^1$ odd graph double and controls its interface flux explicitly. It has no support hypothesis on $K$; the prepared tensor tail and geometry supply the uniform patch bounds used here.

<a id="pm-h-68"></a>
###### The scalar source and its boundary reflection.

In coordinates, absorb the volume density in the second equation and write it as <a id="four:maximal:reg:natural-equation"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:reg:natural-equation}
 \operatorname{div}(\mathcal A DZ+B_1)=E.$$ Here $\mathcal A$ and $B_1$ are the coordinate versions of $3uA_\chi$ and $\lambda uA_\chi K(w,\cdot)$, respectively, with the appropriate homotopy factors in the source. On the established range $\mathcal A$ is bounded, symmetric and uniformly elliptic, and $B_1$ is bounded. The implicit relation for $t$ has derivative $1+pv/3>0$, so $t=t(x,Z,Df)$ is smooth on that range and <a id="four:maximal:reg:t-chain"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:reg:t-chain}
 |Dt|\le C(N)(1+|DZ|+|D^2f|).$$ The quadratic expression for $\mathcal T$, together with the bounded lower-order terms in each stage, therefore gives <a id="four:maximal:reg:coupled-growth"></a>$$\label{four:maximal:reg:coupled-growth}
 |E|\le C(N)(1+|DZ|^2+|D^2f|^2).$$ This estimate does not presume a bound for $DZ$. The prescribed inner conormal value concerns the total flux and is bounded on this range. The outer value of $Z$ is zero.

<a id="four:maximal:reg:reflection-source"></a>
To apply Lemma <a href="#b:lem:natural-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="b:lem:natural-growth">28</a> at a boundary, flatten the face to $x_4=0$, with domain $x_4>0$, and write $Q=\mathcal A DZ+B_1$. Put $R=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,-1)$. For $x_4<0$ set $$\widetilde Z(x)=sZ(Rx),\quad
 \widetilde{\mathcal A}(x)=R\mathcal A(Rx)R,\quad
 \widetilde B_1(x)=sRB_1(Rx),\qquad s\in\{1,-1\}.$$ Then $\widetilde Q(x)=sRQ(Rx)$ below the plane. Its distributional divergence has reflected bulk source $sE(Rx)$ and plane source $$\label{four:maximal:reg:reflection-source}
 (1+s)Q_4^+\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^3\big|_{\{x_4=0\}}.$$ At the inner conormal face use $s=1$. The added signed density is bounded because $Q_4^+$ is the prescribed total conormal flux in these coordinates. At the outer zero Dirichlet face use $s=-1$. The reflected $Z$ is continuous and the normal total flux matches, so there is no plane term. The coefficient matrix remains measurable, symmetric and uniformly elliptic. Each reflected solution is continuous and smooth on its two closed sides. Integration on those sides gives the weak exponential product rule required by the shared lemma, including the full measure in <a href="#four:maximal:reg:reflection-source" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:reg:reflection-source">[four:maximal:reg:reflection-source]</a>.

The absolute source on the doubled patch is consequently dominated by $$C(N)(1+|DZ|^2)\,\mathrm dx+\mu _0,\qquad
 \mu _0=C(N)|D^2f|^2\,\mathrm dx
          +2|Q_4^+|\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^3\big|_{\{x_4=0\}},$$ with the bulk density reflected and the plane term omitted where absent. Equation <a href="#four:maximal:reg:f-hessian-measure" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:reg:f-hessian-measure">[four:maximal:reg:f-hessian-measure]</a> and the area of a three-dimensional plane section give, at every local center, $$\mu _0(B_r(x))\le C(N)r^{2+\beta},\qquad
                         \beta=\min(2\alpha,1)>0.$$ On an interior patch only the bulk term is needed. Thus all the hypotheses of Lemma <a href="#b:lem:natural-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="b:lem:natural-growth">28</a>, with dimension four, hold. Its Hölder representative agrees with the existing continuous $Z$, giving a uniform Hölder bound up to either face.

<a id="pm-h-69"></a>
###### Schauder for the trace equation and the normal datum.

<a id="four:maximal:reg:f-schauder"></a>
The actual coefficients in <a href="#four:maximal:reg:f-normalized" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:reg:f-normalized">[four:maximal:reg:f-normalized]</a> are smooth functions of $x,Z,Df$, including at $Df=0$, since $$A_\chi=\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}-\frac{3+p}{3+pv}\,w\otimes w.$$ Its source is smooth in the same variables and in $f$. The Hölder bounds just proved therefore make them uniformly $C^{0,\theta}$ for some $\theta>0$. Interior and constant Dirichlet Schauder estimates give $$\label{four:maximal:reg:f-schauder}
 \|f\|_{C^{2,\theta}(U')}\le C(N)$$ on smaller patches; the hypotheses are precisely uniform ellipticity, $C^{0,\theta}$ leading coefficients and source, smooth faces and constant Dirichlet data (Gilbarg and Trudinger 2001, secs. 6.1–6.2) <a id="pm-cite-63"></a>[[GilbargTrudinger2001](#ref-GilbargTrudinger2001)].

<a id="four:maximal:reg:Z-nondivergence"></a>
Expand the divergence equation for $Z$ using <a href="#four:maximal:reg:f-schauder" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:reg:f-schauder">[four:maximal:reg:f-schauder]</a>. A derivative of a coefficient depending on $x,Z,Df$ is a bounded term plus bounded multiples of $DZ,D^2f$. Thus it takes the nondivergence form $$\label{four:maximal:reg:Z-nondivergence}
 a^{ij}(x)D_{ij}Z=R_Z,\qquad
 |R_Z|\le C(N)(1+|DZ|^2),$$ with uniformly elliptic $C^{0,\theta}$ leading coefficients. No derivative of $Z$ of order two has been placed on its right side.

<a id="four:maximal:reg:normal-datum"></a>
On an inner face, $f$ is constant and $Df$ is normal, so $A_\chi\nu=\chi\nu$. Dividing the flux condition by $3u\chi>0$ gives $$\label{four:maximal:reg:normal-datum}
 \partial_\nu Z=b(x,Z,f,Df),$$ where $b$ is a smooth bounded-range function, separately on each smooth stage of the homotopy. The formulas agree at stage junctions and have uniform bounds. At zero gradient the smooth formula for $A_\chi$ above gives the same conclusion. A smooth collar extension of the right hand side has derivative bounded by $$C(N)(1+|DZ|+|Df|+|D^2f|)
                         \le C(N)(1+|DZ|).$$ The trace theorem therefore bounds its $W^{1-1/p,p}$ norm on the face by $C(N)(1+\|Z\|_{W^{1,p}})$ on a larger collar patch. In particular, differentiating this extension costs $DZ$ and $D^2f$, and does not cost $D^2Z$.

<a id="pm-h-70"></a>
###### Absorbing the quadratic gradient term.

<a id="four:maximal:reg:Z-linear-estimate"></a>
Fix $p_1>4$. The linear local $W^{2,p_1}$ estimates for <a href="#four:maximal:reg:Z-nondivergence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:reg:Z-nondivergence">[four:maximal:reg:Z-nondivergence]</a>, with zero Dirichlet data or <a href="#four:maximal:reg:normal-datum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:maximal:reg:normal-datum">[four:maximal:reg:normal-datum]</a>, give on nested patches $$\label{four:maximal:reg:Z-linear-estimate}
 \|Z\|_{W^{2,p_1}(U')}
 \le C(N)\left(1+\|DZ\|_{L^{2p_1}(U)}^2
                          +\|Z\|_{W^{1,p_1}(U)}\right).$$ We specify why the coefficient regularity at this point suffices. Freeze the continuous leading matrix on small patches. The constant coefficient interior Hessian estimate follows from the Laplacian estimate by a linear coordinate change. At a boundary, use normal coordinates. On that face the matrix has no mixed tangential-normal entry, by the normal-axis property above. After removing the boundary datum by its Sobolev trace extension, odd Dirichlet or even homogeneous-normal reflection gives the constant coefficient estimate. The term $(a(x)-a(x_0)):D^2Z$ is absorbed when its oscillation is sufficiently small. Cutoff terms are first order. This proves the local estimate with the $W^{1-1/p_1,p_1}$ normal trace norm just estimated; it is the scalar Dirichlet/oblique specialization of (Agmon, Douglis, and Nirenberg 1959, Theorems 15.1–15.3, pp. 702–706, especially Theorem 15.2, estimate (15.5)) <a id="pm-cite-64"></a>[[AgmonDouglisNirenberg1959](#ref-AgmonDouglisNirenberg1959)], together with the interior $L^p$ estimate (Gilbarg and Trudinger 2001, sec. 9.5) <a id="pm-cite-65"></a>[[GilbargTrudinger2001](#ref-GilbargTrudinger2001)]. Uniform Hölder control fixes the patch size uniformly. The complementing condition can also be checked directly: a nonzero decaying Fourier mode for the frozen scalar operator in a half-space has nonzero value and nonzero normal derivative at its boundary. Thus neither the Dirichlet nor the normal operator annihilates that mode. The normal field is smooth and has unit transverse component; the boundary is smooth and the leading coefficients are continuous, as required for this $W^{2,p_1}$ specialization. The inner and outer faces are disjoint, so no change of boundary type occurs within such a patch.

<a id="four:maximal:reg:nirenberg-scaled"></a>
For a ball or smooth half-patch $Q_h$ of radius $h$, subtract a constant from $Z$. Nirenberg’s interpolation inequality, with derivative orders $1,2$, endpoint exponent $\infty$, Hessian exponent $p_1$ and interpolation parameter $1/2$, gives $$\label{four:maximal:reg:nirenberg-scaled}
 \|DZ\|_{L^{2p_1}(Q_h)}^2
